newsitem.title: CANADA: Bank of Canada cuts key rate as economy picks up.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Canada cuts key rate as economy picks up.

text.p: The Bank of Canada on Wednesday lowered its key interest rate for the eighth time this year, raising speculation that the rate-cutting cycle may be coming to an end as Canada's economy gears up for a steady recovery.

"There is no question that the economy did much better in the third quarter than it did in the first half of the year," said Ted Carmichael, senior Canadian analyst with JP Morgan Securities Canada in Toronto.
"But by its action today the Bank seems to be trying to buy additional insurance, to ensure that the economy will continue to grow at a strong rate through year end and into 1997."

The central bank dropped its key bank rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 4.0 percent, a move that prompted major Canadian banks to cut their prime lending rates to 5.5 percent from 5.75, their lowest level since February 1994.

It was the seventh time this year the Bank has cut rates independent of an easing by the Federal Reserve. The Fed's discount rate, at which the central bank lends funds to banking institutions, is at 5.0 percent.
The Bank of Canada has now lowered short-term rates by 200 basis points this year and 425 basis points since May 1995 in a bid to stimulate Canada's sluggish economy.
The Bank's latest move prompted economists to speculate that Canadian short-term interest rates may have reached bottom for the near term.

The cut came on the heels of economic data suggesting that Canadian growth has picked up in the second half. Some analysts said the move was more of an effort to temper a rally in the Canadian dollar than to give the economy another shot in the arm.

The Canadian dollar closed on Wednesday around C$1.3590 (US$0.7358) unchanged from Tuesday's close. Currency traders said the unit was hit by profit-taking soon after the rate ease, but rebounded later.

"The message from the Bank of Canada is loud and clear: A strengthening economy is no impediment to lower rates as long as the Canadian dollar is firming," Nesbitt Burns chief economist Sherry Cooper said in a comment. "While growth is picking up, there is still some slack in the economy."
Earlier this week, Statistics Canada, a government agency, said gross domestic product GDP grew by 0.5 percent in July, surpassing most analysts' expectations and after remaining flat in June.
Michael Manford, chief economist at ScotiaMcLeod, said Wednesday's rate cut would probably be the last in the series, especially if economic data continues to point to a recovery.
"I think that toward the year end the Bank will be definitely neutral," Manford said.
